etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English grand, grond, graund, graunt, from Anglo-Norman graunt, from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grande and grandee.

definitions.definition: Of a large size or extent; great.
Great in size, and fine or imposing in appearance or impression; illustrious, dignified, magnificent.

quote.citation: 1863, Sheridan Le Fanu, The House by the Churchyard:
quote.text: In the mean time, Cluffe had arrived. He was a little bit huffed and grand at being nailed as an evidence, upon a few words carelessly, or, if you will, confidentially dropped at his own mess-table, where Lowe chanced to be a guest; and certainly with no suspicion that his little story could in any way be made to elucidate the mystery of Sturk's murder.

definitions.definition: Having higher rank or more dignity, size, or importance than other persons or things of the same name.
(augmentative) Large, senior (high-ranking), intense, extreme, or exceptional
(usually in compound forms) Standing in the second or some more remote degree of parentage or descent (see grand-).
(Ireland, Northern England, colloquial, otherwise dated) Fine; lovely.
(music) Containing all the parts proper to a given form of composition.
(plural "grand") A thousand of some unit of currency, such as dollars or pounds. (Compare G.)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From granddaughter, grandfather, grandmother, grandson, etc.

quote.text: Once, in Maryland, he met four families of slaves who had all been together for a hundred years: great-grands, grands, mothers, fathers, aunts, uncles, cousins, children.

quote.citation: 2012, Brenda Jackson, Texas Wild & Beyond Temptation, page 47:
quote.text: Her granddaughter and great-granddaughter went with us as chaperones. Did I ever tell you that she had six grands and two great-grands?  […]  And Emily agrees with me it's a shame that I don't even have a grand.
